title: DFS in Reykjavík: Follow the Path, Don’t Look Back
description: Watch DFS carve a route across Reykjavík’s Grandi street graph—one deep detour at a time. In this visualization, the search prioritizes going deeper before backtracking, revealing how DFS explores connected areas.
ig_caption:
🧭🌊 Reykjavík (Grandi) streets, but make it algorithmic! 

🔍 DFS (Depth-First Search) grabs a start node and *dives* down one branch as far as possible before backtracking—perfect for visualizing how recursion/stack behavior shapes exploration.

🗺️ In graph theory terms, we model real streets as a graph: intersections become vertices and road segments become edges (often with direction/weights ignored for pure DFS). DFS uses a LIFO structure (stack or recursion) and a visited set to prevent cycles, meaning the traversal order depends on neighbor ordering—so tiny implementation details can change the route you see. 

⚡ Want to see DFS vs BFS or Dijkstra on the same map grid? Comment your pick and hit follow for more real-map algorithm animations! 

🎬 Watch the full DFS path unfold—then tell me: did it “go too deep” before finding the best way?
fb_caption:
In this reel, we visualize DFS (Depth-First Search) on a real-world street map of Reykjavík’s Grandi district 🌍. DFS is a graph search method that explores as deep as possible along a branch before backtracking, using a stack/recursion + a visited set to avoid loops.

Try it yourself: how does changing neighbor order change the path your DFS chooses? Share this with a friend who loves coding and graph theory, and drop a comment with your start and goal intersection!
